result:
At the edge of a city, where the last apartment blocks give way to vacant lots and scrubby grass, there is often a place that feels unfinished.

Not abandoned, exactly. Abandoned places have a kind of finality to them: broken windows, padlocked doors, weeds claiming the cracks. An unfinished place is different. It still seems to be waiting for instructions.

Maybe there is a half-built road ending in gravel. Maybe there are lamp posts that illuminate nothing but rain. Maybe a bus stop stands beside an empty field, complete with a timetable behind scratched plastic. People use it anyway. Someone always lives farther out than the planners expected.

I like these places because they make the future visible as a physical object. You can see where someone imagined houses, shops, playgrounds, parking spaces, and a clean line of trees. Then something changed: money ran out, permits stalled, a company disappeared, priorities shifted. The map kept going, but the world did not.

In the evening, unfinished places are especially strange. The sky becomes enormous because there are fewer buildings to interrupt it. Cars pass with the sound of brief weather. The lamps turn on one by one, faithfully performing their small duty. Somewhere in the distance, a train moves across the dark like a lit-up idea.

There is comfort in that incompleteness.

Most lives are built this way, after all. We make plans with the confidence of architects, then discover that the land beneath us is softer than we thought. We leave roads leading nowhere. We carry keys for doors that no longer exist. We become experts at living beside empty lots.

And sometimes, years later, someone builds something there. Not what was originally intended—almost never that—but something useful, or beautiful, or at least alive. A bakery. A garden. A cheap apartment with a blue balcony. A little shop that sells batteries, oranges, and lottery tickets.

The unfinished place does not mind.

It has been waiting.
